claim: GpsB is a membrane associated protein that coordinates peptidoglycan synthesis with cell growth and division in the Firmicutes phylum.
source: In the Firmicutes phylum, GpsB is a membrane associated protein that coordinates peptidoglycan synthesis with cell growth and division.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of GpsB function.

claim: The structure, function, and interactome of Staphylococcus aureus GpsB is largely uncharacterized.
source: Although GpsB has been studied in several bacteria, the structure, function, and interactome of Staphylococcus aureus GpsB is largely uncharacterized.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: The crystal structure of the N-terminal domain of S. aureus GpsB was solved.
source: To address this knowledge gap, we solved the crystal structure of the N-terminal domain of S. aureus GpsB, which adopts an atypical, asymmetric dimer, and demonstrates major conformational flexibility that can be mapped to a hinge region formed by a three-residue insertion exclusive to Staphylococci.
evidence: The abstract states that the crystal structure was solved, and crystallographic data is presented in the manuscript.

claim: The N-terminal domain of S. aureus GpsB adopts an atypical, asymmetric dimer.
source: To address this knowledge gap, we solved the crystal structure of the N-terminal domain of S. aureus GpsB, which adopts an atypical, asymmetric dimer, and demonstrates major conformational flexibility that can be mapped to a hinge region formed by a three-residue insertion exclusive to Staphylococci.
evidence: The crystal structure shows an asymmetric dimer arrangement, as described in the abstract and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The N-terminal domain of S. aureus GpsB demonstrates major conformational flexibility that can be mapped to a hinge region formed by a three-residue insertion exclusive to Staphylococci.
source: To address this knowledge gap, we solved the crystal structure of the N-terminal domain of S. aureus GpsB, which adopts an atypical, asymmetric dimer, and demonstrates major conformational flexibility that can be mapped to a hinge region formed by a three-residue insertion exclusive to Staphylococci.
evidence: The abstract describes conformational flexibility mapped to a hinge region, supported by crystallographic data (Figure 1B), NMR data (Figure 1C), and MD simulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).

claim: When the three-residue insertion is excised, the thermal stability of GpsB increases.
source: When this three-residue insertion is excised, its thermal stability increases, and the mutant no longer produces a previously reported lethal phenotype when overexpressed in Bacillus subtilis.
evidence: The abstract states increased thermal stability, which is supported by circular dichroism data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The GpsB mutant lacking the three-residue insertion no longer produces a previously reported lethal phenotype when overexpressed in Bacillus subtilis.
source: When this three-residue insertion is excised, its thermal stability increases, and the mutant no longer produces a previously reported lethal phenotype when overexpressed in Bacillus subtilis.
evidence: The abstract states the loss of lethal phenotype, which is demonstrated by growth assays in Figure 2C.

claim: In S. aureus, hinge mutants of GpsB are less functional.
source: In S. aureus, we show that these hinge mutants are less functional and speculate that the conformational flexibility imparted by the hinge region may serve as a dynamic switch to fine-tune the function of the GpsB complex and/or to promote interaction with its various partners.
evidence: The abstract states reduced functionality, supported by growth assays and microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The conformational flexibility imparted by the hinge region may serve as a dynamic switch to fine-tune the function of the GpsB complex and/or to promote interaction with its various partners.
source: In S. aureus, we show that these hinge mutants are less functional and speculate that the conformational flexibility imparted by the hinge region may serve as a dynamic switch to fine-tune the function of the GpsB complex and/or to promote interaction with its various partners.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation in the abstract.

claim: The N-terminal domain of GpsB binds PBP4.
source: Furthermore, we provide the first biochemical, biophysical, and crystallographic evidence that the N-terminal domain of GpsB binds not only PBP4, but also FtsZ, through a conserved recognition motif located on their C-termini, thus coupling peptidoglycan synthesis to cell division.
evidence: The abstract states this binding is demonstrated through multiple methods, supported by SPR data (Figure 4A) and crystal structure (Figure 4B).

claim: The N-terminal domain of GpsB binds FtsZ.
source: Furthermore, we provide the first biochemical, biophysical, and crystallographic evidence that the N-terminal domain of GpsB binds not only PBP4, but also FtsZ, through a conserved recognition motif located on their C-termini, thus coupling peptidoglycan synthesis to cell division.
evidence: The abstract states this binding is demonstrated through multiple methods, supported by SPR data (Figure 3B), GTPase assay (Figure 3C), and NMR data (Figure 3D).

claim: GpsB binds PBP4 and FtsZ through a conserved recognition motif located on their C-termini.
source: Furthermore, we provide the first biochemical, biophysical, and crystallographic evidence that the N-terminal domain of GpsB binds not only PBP4, but also FtsZ, through a conserved recognition motif located on their C-termini, thus coupling peptidoglycan synthesis to cell division.
evidence: The abstract states binding occurs through C-terminal recognition motifs, supported by sequence alignment (Figure 3A) and structural data (Figure 4B).

claim: The interaction of GpsB with FtsZ and PBP4 couples peptidoglycan synthesis to cell division.
source: Furthermore, we provide the first biochemical, biophysical, and crystallographic evidence that the N-terminal domain of GpsB binds not only PBP4, but also FtsZ, through a conserved recognition motif located on their C-termini, thus coupling peptidoglycan synthesis to cell division.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the binding data in the abstract.

claim: FtsZ is a bacterial homolog of eukaryotic tubulin.
source: Perhaps the most important and well-studied divisomal protein is FtsZ, a bacterial homolog of eukaryotic tubulin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: FtsZ marks the division site by forming a 'Z-ring' in association with early-stage divisomal proteins such as FtsA, ZapA, SepF, and EzrA in Gram-positive bacteria.
source: FtsZ marks the division site by forming a 'Z-ring' in association with early-stage divisomal proteins such as FtsA, ZapA, SepF, and EzrA in Gram-positive bacteria (Gamba et al., 2009; Lutkenhaus et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: GpsB is a DivIVA-like protein that is highly conserved in Firmicutes.
source: GpsB is a DivIVA-like protein that is highly conserved in Firmicutes (Halbedel and Lewis, 2019; Hammond et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: GpsB is dispensable or conditionally essential in most Firmicutes.
source: While GpsB is dispensable, or conditionally essential in most Firmicutes (Rismondo et al., 2016; Fleurie et al., 2014; Claessen et al., 2008; Tavares et al., 2008), it was reported to be essential for growth in Staphylococcus aureus (Santiago et al., 2015; Gillaspy, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: GpsB was reported to be essential for growth in Staphylococcus aureus.
source: While GpsB is dispensable, or conditionally essential in most Firmicutes (Rismondo et al., 2016; Fleurie et al., 2014; Claessen et al., 2008; Tavares et al., 2008), it was reported to be essential for growth in Staphylococcus aureus (Santiago et al., 2015; Gillaspy, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent studies indicate that gpsB may not be essential in S. aureus, but nevertheless plays a significant role in maintaining S. aureus cell morphology.
source: However, recent studies indicate that gpsB may not be essential, but nevertheless plays a significant role in maintaining S. aureus cell morphology (Sutton et al., 2023; Bartlett et al., 2023; Costa et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated with citations to recent studies.

claim: S. aureus GpsB has a unique ability to regulate FtsZ polymerization in S. aureus.
source: In particular, the importance of S. aureus GpsB (Sa GpsB) for cell division is underscored by its unique ability to regulate FtsZ polymerization in S. aureus (Eswara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: GpsB-FtsZ interaction has not been reported in bacteria other than S. aureus.
source: At this time, GpsB-FtsZ interaction has not been reported in other bacteria.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Sa GpsB has been reported to interact with EzrA.
source: Sa GpsB has also been reported to interact with other cell division proteins such as EzrA (Steele et al., 2011), DivIVA (Bottomley et al., 2017), and the wall teichoic acids (WTA) biosynthesis/export proteins TarO and TarG (Kent, 2024; Hammond et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Sa GpsB has been reported to interact with DivIVA.
source: Sa GpsB has also been reported to interact with other cell division proteins such as EzrA (Steele et al., 2011), DivIVA (Bottomley et al., 2017), and the wall teichoic acids (WTA) biosynthesis/export proteins TarO and TarG (Kent, 2024; Hammond et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Sa GpsB has been reported to interact with TarO.
source: Sa GpsB has also been reported to interact with other cell division proteins such as EzrA (Steele et al., 2011), DivIVA (Bottomley et al., 2017), and the wall teichoic acids (WTA) biosynthesis/export proteins TarO and TarG (Kent, 2024; Hammond et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Sa GpsB has been reported to interact with TarG.
source: Sa GpsB has also been reported to interact with other cell division proteins such as EzrA (Steele et al., 2011), DivIVA (Bottomley et al., 2017), and the wall teichoic acids (WTA) biosynthesis/export proteins TarO and TarG (Kent, 2024; Hammond et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: GpsB binds to a short, ~5- to 30-residue N-terminal sequence found on the cytosolic region of bitopic PBPs, referred to as an N-terminal 'mini-domain'.
source: These studies show that GpsB binds to a short, ~5- to 30-residue N-terminal sequence found on the cytosolic region of these bitopic PBPs, referred to as an N-terminal 'mini-domain' (Rismondo et al., 2016; Cleverley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: PBP mini-domains containing an (S/T)-R-X-X-R-(R/K) motif directly interact with the N-terminal domain of GpsB by forming electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonds with a shallow, acidic cavity located at the GpsB dimer interface.
source: Cleverley et al. found PBP mini-domains containing an (S/T)-R-X-X-R-(R/K) motif directly interact with the N-terminal domain of GpsB by forming electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonds with a shallow, acidic cavity located at the GpsB dimer interface (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) Cleverley et al., 2019.
evidence: This is stated with a citation and reference to figure supplement showing the interaction.

claim: S. aureus has only four annotated PBPs: PBP1, PBP2, PBP3, and PBP4.
source: While Lm, Sp, and Bs have at least six annotated PBPs (Kocaoglu et al., 2015; Korsak et al., 2010; Kunst et al., 1997), there are only four in S. aureus: PBP1, PBP2, PBP3, and PBP4 (Gillaspy, 2006) - five in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) which expresses an additional β-lactam insensitive PBP, PBP2a (Hartman and Tomasz, 1984).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) has five PBPs, including an additional β-lactam insensitive PBP, PBP2a.
source: While Lm, Sp, and Bs have at least six annotated PBPs (Kocaoglu et al., 2015; Korsak et al., 2010; Kunst et al., 1997), there are only four in S. aureus: PBP1, PBP2, PBP3, and PBP4 (Gillaspy, 2006) - five in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) which expresses an additional β-lactam insensitive PBP, PBP2a (Hartman and Tomasz, 1984).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: S. aureus is distinguished by its highly cross-linked peptidoglycan and can readily become resistant to β-lactams via PBP4 and the acquisition of PBP2a.
source: S. aureus is further distinguished by its highly cross-linked peptidoglycan and can readily become resistant to β-lactams via PBP4 and the acquisition of PBP2a (Łeski and Tomasz, 2005; Snowden and Perkins, 1990).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The β-lactam-resistant phenotype relies on WTA assembly, which influences the function and localization of PBP4 and PBP2a.
source: It is believed this β-lactam-resistant phenotype relies on WTA assembly, which influences the function and localization of PBP4 and PBP2a (Atilano et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: PBP4 has recently been found to contribute to β-lactam insensitivity.
source: While PBP2a is a historically recognized element of antibacterial resistance, PBP4 has recently been found to contribute to β-lactam insensitivity (Chatterjee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: PBP4 is the sole class C PBP in S. aureus.
source: As the sole class C PBP in S. aureus, PBP4 bears the fold and architecture of a carboxypeptidase, but uniquely catalyzes both transpeptidase and carboxypeptidase reactions (Finan et al., 2001; Henze and Berger-Bächi, 1995; Navratna et al., 2010; Wyke et al., 1981).
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of PBP4.

claim: PBP4 bears the fold and architecture of a carboxypeptidase, but uniquely catalyzes both transpeptidase and carboxypeptidase reactions.
source: As the sole class C PBP in S. aureus, PBP4 bears the fold and architecture of a carboxypeptidase, but uniquely catalyzes both transpeptidase and carboxypeptidase reactions (Finan et al., 2001; Henze and Berger-Bächi, 1995; Navratna et al., 2010; Wyke et al., 1981).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The crystal structure of the N-terminal domain (residues 1–70) of Sa GpsB was solved at 1.95 Å resolution in the P21 space group.
source: Using X-ray crystallography, we solved the structure of the N-terminal domain (residues 1–70) of Sa GpsB at 1.95 Å resolution in the P21 space group (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1), with four monomers per asymmetric unit forming two dimers (dimers A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to crystallographic data.

claim: The asymmetric unit of Sa GpsB N-terminal domain contains four monomers forming two dimers.
source: Using X-ray crystallography, we solved the structure of the N-terminal domain (residues 1–70) of Sa GpsB at 1.95 Å resolution in the P21 space group (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1), with four monomers per asymmetric unit forming two dimers (dimers A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to crystallographic data.

claim: The overall structure of Sa GpsB is similar to previously determined GpsB orthologs.
source: The overall structure of GpsB is similar to previously determined GpsB orthologs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Rismondo et al., 2016; Cleverley et al., 2019) and retains the same fold of DivIVA (Oliva et al., 2010), though it shares much less sequence similarity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to figure supplement showing structural comparison.

claim: Sa GpsB retains the same fold of DivIVA, though it shares much less sequence similarity.
source: The overall structure of GpsB is similar to previously determined GpsB orthologs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Rismondo et al., 2016; Cleverley et al., 2019) and retains the same fold of DivIVA (Oliva et al., 2010), though it shares much less sequence similarity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and reference to sequence alignment figure.

claim: Dimerization of the GpsB N-terminal domain is facilitated by a pattern of nonpolar residues every three to four residues, promoting the formation of a hydrophobic core in the coiled-coil.
source: Dimerization of the N-terminal domain is facilitated by a pattern of nonpolar residues every three to four residues, promoting the formation of a hydrophobic core in the coiled-coil.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The N-terminal domain of Sa GpsB is partitioned into three regions: a relatively short α-helix with approximately two turns (residues 10–16), a second longer α-helix (residues 28–70) that forms a coiled-coil, and an amphipathic 10-residue loop (residues 17–27) that links these two helices and intertwines with the adjacent protomer.
source: This N-terminal domain is partitioned into three regions: a relatively short α-helix with approximately two turns (residues 10–16), a second longer α-helix (residues 28–70) that forms a coiled-coil, and an amphipathic 10-residue loop (residues 17–27) that links these two helices and intertwines with the adjacent protomer, 'capping' GpsB (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a structural description with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The loop region (residues 17–27) is proposed to interact with the inner leaflet of the cell membrane.
source: This loop region is proposed to interact with the inner leaflet of the cell membrane (Halbedel and Lewis, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Sa GpsB protomers bend at a hinge region, adopting pitch angles (θ) of 137–140° (dimer A) and 156–166° (dimer B).
source: The most unique structural feature of Sa GpsB is a hinge forming at the midpoint of its N-terminal domain that causes each protomer to bend, adopting pitch angles (θ) of 137–140° (dimer A) and 156–166° (dimer B).
evidence: This is stated with reference to structural measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GpsB protomers from Lm, Bs, Sp, and Sa DivIVA are almost linear (θ=167–179°) and practically indistinguishable when superimposed.
source: In contrast, GpsB protomers from Lm, Bs, Sp, and Sa DivIVA are almost linear (θ=167–179°) and practically indistinguishable when superimposed (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated with reference to structural comparison shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There is a 3-amino acid insertion in the Sa GpsB sequence where the helicity is disrupted and a cluster of four Met residues (Met45, Met48) are interlocked at the dimer interface at this position.
source: We find that there is a 3-amino acid insertion in the Sa GpsB sequence where the helicity is disrupted and that a cluster of four Met residues (Met45, Met48) are interlocked at the dimer interface at this position (Figure 1B; dotted rectangle).
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The Met residues at the hinge region are only found in Staphylococci.
source: These Met residues are only found in Staphylococci (Figure 1E) and take the place of an aromatic Tyr or Phe present in other orthologs, which normally stabilize the core via π stacking interactions.
evidence: This is stated with reference to sequence alignment shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The 3-amino acid insertion likely disrupts the continuity of the coiled-coil.
source: While the 3-amino acid insertion likely disrupts the continuity of the coiled-coil, methionine is one of the most flexible aliphatic amino acids and may further contribute to the conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from structural observations.

claim: Methionine is one of the most flexible aliphatic amino acids and may further contribute to the conformational flexibility of Sa GpsB.
source: While the 3-amino acid insertion likely disrupts the continuity of the coiled-coil, methionine is one of the most flexible aliphatic amino acids and may further contribute to the conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on known properties of methionine.

claim: Solution state NMR spectroscopy supports the notion of intrinsic conformational heterogeneity in Sa GpsB.
source: Experiments using solution state NMR spectroscopy further support the notion of intrinsic conformational heterogeneity, suggesting it is a bona fide structural feature rather than a crystallization artifact.
evidence: This is stated with reference to NMR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The 2D 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of Sa GpsBWT1-70 shows 100 well-resolved backbone amide signals instead of the expected 72.
source: The Sa GpsBWT1-70 construct contains a two-residue N-terminal extension (GH) after removal of the purification tag, and thus a total of 72 signals are expected. The 2D 1H-15N HSQC spectrum shows good signal dispersion (Figure 1C), which is characteristic of a folded domain. However, a total of 100 well-resolved backbone amide signals are observed, and seven pairs of signals are detected in the Asn/Gln sidechain region instead of four pairs (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated with reference to NMR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Seven pairs of signals are detected in the Asn/Gln sidechain region of the 1H-15N HSQC spectrum instead of four pairs.
source: The Sa GpsBWT1-70 construct contains a two-residue N-terminal extension (GH) after removal of the purification tag, and thus a total of 72 signals are expected. The 2D 1H-15N HSQC spectrum shows good signal dispersion (Figure 1C), which is characteristic of a folded domain. However, a total of 100 well-resolved backbone amide signals are observed, and seven pairs of signals are detected in the Asn/Gln sidechain region instead of four pairs (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated with reference to NMR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The appearance of additional signals in the NMR spectrum is not due to proline cis/trans isomerization since there are no prolines in the sequence.
source: The appearance of the additional signals is not due to proline cis/trans isomerization since there are no prolines in the sequence, nor is it due to self-aggregation of the dimers to form a dimer-of-dimers or higher order oligomers, because raising the concentration from 160 to 700 μM has no effect on the number of signals in the spectrum (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from sequence analysis and NMR data.

claim: The appearance of additional signals in the NMR spectrum is not due to self-aggregation of the dimers because raising the concentration from 160 to 700 μM has no effect on the number of signals.
source: The appearance of the additional signals is not due to proline cis/trans isomerization since there are no prolines in the sequence, nor is it due to self-aggregation of the dimers to form a dimer-of-dimers or higher order oligomers, because raising the concentration from 160 to 700 μM has no effect on the number of signals in the spectrum (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated with reference to concentration-dependent NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The 1H-15N HSQC of Sa GpsBWT1-70 exhibits differential linewidths, with a set of 13 narrow signals at the center of the spectrum where disordered segments appear, and a larger set of 87 signals dispersed throughout the spectrum.
source: In addition, the 1H-15N HSQC of Sa GpsBWT1-70 exhibits differential linewidths, with a set of 13 narrow signals at the center of the spectrum where disordered segments appear, and a larger set of 87 signals dispersed throughout the spectrum.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from NMR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of narrow signals in the NMR spectrum corresponds well with the number of residues found at the flexible N-terminus, suggesting that the appearance of extra signals is due to sampling of multiple conformations of the coiled-coil.
source: The number of the narrow signals corresponds well with the number of residues found at the flexible N-terminus, suggesting that the appearance of extra signals is due to sampling of multiple conformations of the coiled-coil.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from NMR data.

claim: Three of the four Asn/Gln sidechain pairs showing chemical shift degeneracy are adjacent to the hinge, providing strong evidence that the observed conformational heterogeneity occurs at this region.
source: Furthermore, three of the four Asn/Gln sidechain pairs showing chemical shift degeneracy are adjacent to the hinge (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) providing strong evidence that the observed conformational heterogeneity occurs at this region.
evidence: This is stated with reference to structural mapping shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations support the idea that conformational flexibility exists in solution for Sa GpsB.
source: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using Gromacs v. 5.0.4 and a CHARMM36m force field also support the idea that conformational flexibility exists in solution.
evidence: This is stated with reference to MD simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: After approximately 100 ns of MD simulation, dimer 1 of Sa GpsB adopts an ~180° pitch angle that occurs concomitantly to major fluctuations in dimer 2 in a separate simulation.
source: After approximately 100 ns, dimer 1 adopts an ~180° pitch angle that occurs concomitantly to major fluctuations in dimer 2 in a separate simulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), although the preference for continuous helical structures (corresponding to ~180° pitch angles) may sometimes be influenced by specific force field parameters.
evidence: This is stated with reference to MD simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Deleting either MAD or MNN produces a homology model where residues 45–70, normally displaced by one turn, are now aligned with their orthologous residue pair.
source: Deleting either MAD or MNN produces a homology model where residues 45–70, normally displaced by one turn, are now aligned with their orthologous residue pair (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated with reference to homology model shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The Tm of Sa GpsBΔMAD1-70 (38.88 ± 0.18°C) was modestly higher than Sa GpsBWT1-70 (34.63 ± 0.33°C).
source: Perhaps the most notable finding from this experiment was that, while the Tm of Sa GpsBΔMAD1-70 (38.88 ± 0.18°C) was only modestly higher than Sa GpsBWT1-70 (34.63 ± 0.33°C), the Tm of Sa GpsBΔMNN1-70 (53.65 ± 0.55°C) was highly stable, approximately 1.5-fold higher than that of Sa GpsBWT1-70 and comparable to the thermal stability of the full-length Sa GpsBWTFL.
evidence: This is stated with reference to CD data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Tm of Sa GpsBΔMNN1-70 (53.65 ± 0.55°C) was approximately 1.5-fold higher than that of Sa GpsBWT1-70 and comparable to the thermal stability of the full-length Sa GpsBWTFL.
source: Perhaps the most notable finding from this experiment was that, while the Tm of Sa GpsBΔMAD1-70 (38.88 ± 0.18°C) was only modestly higher than Sa GpsBWT1-70 (34.63 ± 0.33°C), the Tm of Sa GpsBΔMNN1-70 (53.65 ± 0.55°C) was highly stable, approximately 1.5-fold higher than that of Sa GpsBWT1-70 and comparable to the thermal stability of the full-length Sa GpsBWTFL.
evidence: This is stated with reference to CD data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The conformational properties of the Sa GpsBΔMAD1-70 mutant are different from wildtype when analyzed by 1H-15N HSQC.
source: The conformational properties of the Sa GpsBΔMAD1-70 mutant were also different when analyzed by 1H-15N HSQC (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated with reference to NMR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Most of the dispersed signals from the coiled-coil region of Sa GpsBΔMAD1-70 experience severe broadening, in many cases beyond detection, as well as changes in chemical shift.
source: Most of the dispersed signals from the coiled-coil region experience severe broadening, in many cases beyond detection, as well as changes in chemical shift, while all narrow signals at the center of the spectrum show no change in linewidth or positions.
evidence: This is stated with reference to NMR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Signal broadening in Sa GpsBΔMAD1-70 is caused by changes in the rate of interconversion between the available conformations from the intermediate-slow for WT (s) to the intermediate-fast exchange regime for ΔMAD (ms).
source: Signal broadening is caused by changes in the rate of interconversion between the available conformations from the intermediate-slow for WT (s) to the intermediate-fast exchange regime for ΔMAD (ms), but without altering the overall number of states, as seven pairs of Asn/Gln sidechain pairs of signals are observed.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of NMR data.

claim: Conformational rigidity is a well-established correlate of thermal stability.
source: Conformational rigidity is a well-established correlate of thermal stability (Karshikoff et al., 2015), and may contribute to the enhanced Tm of Sa GpsBΔMNN and Sa GpsBΔMAD.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to established knowledge.

claim: The homology model corresponding to Sa GpsBΔMNN and Sa GpsBΔMAD reveals several residues potentially form stronger interactions than the WT.
source: The aforementioned homology model (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) corresponding to Sa GpsBΔMNN and Sa GpsBΔMAD reveals several residues potentially form stronger interactions than the WT.
evidence: This is stated with reference to homology model shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: An intrahelical electrostatic interaction replaces a potential repulsion between Asp47 and Glu51 with Asn47/Lys51 in Sa GpsBΔMAD and Asp47/Lys51 in Sa GpsBΔMNN.
source: These include an intrahelical electrostatic interaction that replaces a potential repulsion between Asp47 and Glu51 with Asn47/Lys51 in Sa GpsBΔMAD and Asp47/Lys51 in Sa GpsBΔMNN (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is stated with reference to homology model shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The favorable Asp47/Lys51 electrostatic interactions in GpsBΔMNN may further contribute to its higher thermostability.
source: The favorable Asp47/Lys51 electrostatic interactions in GpsBΔMNN may further contribute to its higher thermostability.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on structural modeling.

claim: Overproduction of Sa GpsB in B. subtilis causes cell division arrest which eventually leads to filamentation and cell lysis.
source: Previously, we reported that overproduction of Sa GpsB in B. subtilis causes cell division arrest which eventually leads to filamentation and cell lysis (Eswara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Overproduction of Bs GpsB is not lethal in B. subtilis.
source: As previously established, overproduction of Bs GpsB is not lethal, but Sa GpsB is (Figure 2C; Eswara et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to growth assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Overproduction of Sa GpsB is lethal in B. subtilis.
source: As previously established, overproduction of Bs GpsB is not lethal, but Sa GpsB is (Figure 2C; Eswara et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to growth assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Overproduction of either ΔMAD or ΔMNN Sa GpsB is not lethal in B. subtilis and cells grow as well as the negative controls.
source: In contrast, overproduction of either ΔMAD or ΔMNN Sa GpsB is not lethal and cells grow as well as the negative controls (B. subtilis WT and inducible Bs GpsB strain).
evidence: This is stated with reference to growth assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The hinge region of Sa GpsB, characterized by two Met residues, is essential for the normal function of Sa GpsB as assessed by lethal phenotype in B. subtilis.
source: These results suggest the hinge region of Sa GpsB, characterized by two Met residues (Figure 1B), is essential for the normal function of Sa GpsB as assessed by lethal phenotype in B. subtilis.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from growth assay data.

claim: Bs GpsB-GFP localizes to the division site in B. subtilis.
source: As reported previously, and as shown in Figure 2D, Bs GpsB-GFP localizes to the division site (Claessen et al., 2008; Tavares et al., 2008; Hammond et al., 2022) and does not lead to filamentation upon overproduction (2.09 ±0.49 µm; n=50), but Sa GpsB-GFP forms foci throughout the entire cell, and causes severe filamentation (22.83 ±16.51 µm; n=21) (Eswara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Bs GpsB-GFP does not lead to filamentation upon overproduction in B. subtilis (2.09 ±0.49 µm; n=50).
source: As reported previously, and as shown in Figure 2D, Bs GpsB-GFP localizes to the division site (Claessen et al., 2008; Tavares et al., 2008; Hammond et al., 2022) and does not lead to filamentation upon overproduction (2.09 ±0.49 µm; n=50), but Sa GpsB-GFP forms foci throughout the entire cell, and causes severe filamentation (22.83 ±16.51 µm; n=21) (Eswara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with reference to microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sa GpsB-GFP forms foci throughout the entire cell and causes severe filamentation in B. subtilis (22.83 ±16.51 µm; n=21).
source: As reported previously, and as shown in Figure 2D, Bs GpsB-GFP localizes to the division site (Claessen et al., 2008; Tavares et al., 2008; Hammond et al., 2022) and does not lead to filamentation upon overproduction (2.09 ±0.49 µm; n=50), but Sa GpsB-GFP forms foci throughout the entire cell, and causes severe filamentation (22.83 ±16.51 µm; n=21) (Eswara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and reference to microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ΔMAD and ΔMNN variants of Sa GpsB-GFP do not cause filamentation in B. subtilis (2.13 ±0.44 µm and 2.10 ±0.43 µm respectively; n=50) and are clearly localized at the division site.
source: However, ΔMAD and ΔMNN variants of Sa GpsB-GFP do not cause filamentation (2.13 ±0.44 µm and 2.10 ±0.43 µm respectively; n=50) and are clearly localized at the division site.
evidence: This is stated with reference to microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ΔMAD and ΔMNN mutants presumably interact with the B. subtilis cell division machinery to allow for division site localization, but fail to elicit lethal filamentation and toxicity.
source: Taken together, this data suggests the ΔMAD and ΔMNN mutants presumably interact with the B. subtilis cell division machinery to allow for division site localization, but fail to elicit lethal filamentation and toxicity (Eswara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from microscopy and growth assay data.

claim: Overproduction of Sa GpsB leads to a 100- to 1000-fold growth inhibition compared to empty vector control in S. aureus.
source: Overproduction of Sa GpsB leads to a 100- to 1000-fold growth inhibition compared to EV control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated with reference to growth assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells overproducing Sa GpsBΔMNN grew similarly to the empty vector control in S. aureus.
source: Interestingly, while cells overproducing Sa GpsBΔMNN grew similarly to the EV control, Sa gpsBΔMAD overexpression resulted in growth inhibition comparable to Sa GpsB.
evidence: This is stated with reference to growth assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sa gpsBΔMAD overexpression resulted in growth inhibition comparable to Sa GpsB in S. aureus.
source: Interestingly, while cells overproducing Sa GpsBΔMNN grew similarly to the EV control, Sa gpsBΔMAD overexpression resulted in growth inhibition comparable to Sa GpsB.
evidence: This is stated with reference to growth assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The affinity of Sa GpsBΔMNN to itself appears to be greater compared to Sa GpsBΔMNN and Sa GpsB.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, the affinity of Sa GpsBΔMNN to itself appears to be greater compared to Sa GpsBΔMNN and Sa GpsB.
evidence: This is stated with reference to bacterial two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sa GpsBΔMAD appears to have similar affinity to itself and Sa GpsB, but it is weaker compared to the self-interaction of Sa GpsB.
source: Sa GpsBΔMAD appears to have similar affinity to itself and Sa GpsB, but it is weaker compared to the self-interaction of Sa GpsB.
evidence: This is stated with reference to bacterial two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The differential affinity between mutant Sa GpsB and WT Sa GpsB could underlie the observed difference in phenotypes.
source: Thus, the differential affinity between mutant Sa GpsB and WT Sa GpsB could underlie the observed difference in phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from bacterial two-hybrid data.

claim: Overproduction of Sa GpsB leads to cell size enlargement due to cell division inhibition in S. aureus.
source: As we have previously shown, overproduction of Sa GpsB leads to cell size enlargement due to cell division inhibition (Eswara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cells overproducing Sa GpsB show an increase in cell diameter (1.00 ±0.19 µm) when compared to the empty vector control (0.90 ±0.13 µm) in S. aureus.
source: Using fluorescence microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), we re-confirmed the increase in cell diameter in cells overproducing Sa GpsB (1.00 ±0.19 µm) when compared to the EV control (0.90 ±0.13 µm).
evidence: This is stated with reference to microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Cells overproducing Sa GpsBΔMAD displayed a statistically significant increase in cell diameter (0.95 ±0.16 µm) in S. aureus.
source: In agreement with the lethal plate phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), cells overproducing Sa GpsBΔMAD also displayed a statistically significant increase in cell diameter (0.95 ±0.16 µm), while Sa GpsBΔMNN did not (0.91 ±0.15 µm) and resembled EV control.
evidence: This is stated with reference to microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Sa GpsBΔMNN did not show a statistically significant increase in cell diameter (0.91 ±0.15 µm) and resembled empty vector control in S. aureus.
source: In agreement with the lethal plate phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), cells overproducing Sa GpsBΔMAD also displayed a statistically significant increase in cell diameter (0.95 ±0.16 µm), while Sa GpsBΔMNN did not (0.91 ±0.15 µm) and resembled EV control.
evidence: This is stated with reference to microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Both ΔMAD and ΔMNN mutants of Sa GpsB localize to the division site in S. aureus.
source: Lastly, by GFP tagging, we observed that both mutants localize to the division site similar to Sa GpsB-GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F; Eswara et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ΔMNN is less functional compared to ΔMAD in terms of causing growth inhibition on plate and cell enlargement phenotype in S. aureus.
source: In summary, ΔMNN is less functional compared to ΔMAD in terms of causing growth inhibition on plate and cell enlargement phenotype, however both ΔMAD and ΔMNN mutants are able to localize to division sites.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of experimental observations.

claim: Sa gpsBΔMAD appears to be less toxic compared to the inducible WT Sa gpsB when expressed as the sole copy in S. aureus ΔgpsB background.
source: As the sole copy, Sa gpsBΔMAD appears to be less toxic compared to the inducible WT Sa gpsB, suggesting that it is partially functional (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated with reference to growth assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The ability of Sa gpsBΔMNN to impact S. aureus growth is severely impaired and resembles the empty vector control.
source: However, the ability of Sa gpsBΔMNN to impact S. aureus growth is severely impaired and resembles the EV control.
evidence: This is stated with reference to growth assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Co-expression of hinge region mutants does not completely abolish the toxicity of Sa gpsB-gfp in B. subtilis.
source: We observed that co-expression of hinge region mutants does not completely abolish the toxicity of Sa gpsB-gfp (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated with reference to growth assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Although the Sa gpsBΔMAD and Sa gpsBΔMNN mutants are by themselves nonfunctional in B. subtilis, they do not drastically inhibit the function of WT GpsB in the heteromer.
source: This result suggests that, although the Sa gpsBΔMAD and Sa gpsBΔMNN mutants are by themselves nonfunctional in B. subtilis (Figure 2C), they do not drastically inhibit the function of WT GpsB in the heteromer.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from co-expression data.

claim: The deletion mutants lacking the flexible hinge region may to some degree potentially mimic certain GpsB conformations with varied activities.
source: We hypothesize that the deletion mutants lacking the flexible hinge region may to some degree potentially mimic certain GpsB conformations with varied activities.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on experimental observations.

claim: The protomers adopting different conformations within the GpsB complex can function independently of one another, providing a mechanism to fine-tune the function of the whole complex.
source: Thus the new data may indicate that the protomers adopting different conformations within the GpsB complex can function independently of one another, providing a mechanism to fine-tune the function of the whole complex.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of experimental data.

claim: GpsB directly interacts with Sa FtsZ to stimulate its GTPase activity and modulate its polymerization characteristics.
source: We previously demonstrated that GpsB directly interacts with Sa FtsZ to stimulate its GTPase activity and modulate its polymerization characteristics (Eswara et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: The last 12 residues of Sa FtsZ (N-R-E-E-R-R—S-R-R-T-R-R) are a repeated match of the consensus GpsB-binding motif (S/T-R-X-X-R-(R/K)) found in the N-termini of Bs PBP1, Lm PBPA1, and Sp PBP2a.
source: Remarkably, we discovered that the last 12 residues of Sa FtsZ (N-R-E-E-R-R—S-R-R-T-R-R), also known as the C-terminal variable (CTV) region (Buske and Levin, 2012), are a repeated match of the consensus GpsB-binding motif (S/T-R-X-X-R-(R/K)) found in the N-termini of Bs PBP1, Lm PBPA1, and Sp PBP2a.
evidence: This is stated as a discovery from sequence analysis.

claim: The interaction between GpsB and FtsZ is unique to S. aureus.
source: To our knowledge, the interaction between GpsB and FtsZ is unique to S. aureus (Hammond et al., 2019), which is consistent with the absence of this motif in FtsZ orthologs from other organisms (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and reference to sequence alignment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sa FtsZ (residues 325–390) binds to full-length Sa GpsB with a KD of 40.21 ± 1.77 µM.
source: To initially test whether the predicted FtsZ GpsB-binding motif directly binds to Sa GpsB, we purified and titrated the terminal 66 residues of Sa FtsZ (325–390) against full-length Sa GpsB using surface plasmon resonance (SPR), revealing a dose-dependent interaction (KD = 40.21 ± 1.77 µM; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated with reference to SPR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sa FtsZ (residues 325–390) binds exclusively to the Sa GpsB N-terminal domain (1–70) with a KD of 40.22 ± 1.38 µM.
source: A simultaneous titration against only the Sa GpsB N-terminal domain (1–70) demonstrates that the C-terminus of Sa FtsZ binds exclusively to this domain (KD = 40.22 ± 1.38 µM).
evidence: This is stated with reference to SPR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sa FtsZ CTV (379–390) binds to Sa GpsB with a KD of 73.63 ± 9.43 µM.
source: This is further supported by assays with Sa FtsZ CTV (379–390; KD = 73.63 ± 9.43 µM) and the final eight residues of Sa FtsZ (383–390; KD 17.76±1.25 µM).
evidence: This is stated with reference to SPR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The final eight residues of Sa FtsZ (383–390) bind to Sa GpsB with a KD of 17.76±1.25 µM.
source: This is further supported by assays with Sa FtsZ CTV (379–390; KD = 73.63 ± 9.43 µM) and the final eight residues of Sa FtsZ (383–390; KD 17.76±1.25 µM).
evidence: This is stated with reference to SPR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The approximate fourfold difference in affinity between the CTV and the final eight residues of FtsZ could be a result of the inclusion of two Glu residues in the CTV (E381, E382), which may experience repulsion from the negatively charged PBP-binding pocket of GpsB.
source: The approximate fourfold difference in affinity between the CTV and the final eight residues could be a result of the inclusion of two Glu residues in the CTV (E381, E382), which may experience repulsion from the negatively charged PBP-binding pocket of GpsB.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on SPR data and structural knowledge.

claim: Addition of Sa GpsB enhanced the GTPase activity of Sa FtsZ.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, and as reported previously, addition of Sa GpsB enhanced the GTPase activity of Sa FtsZ.
evidence: This is stated with reference to GTPase assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The GpsB-mediated enhancement of GTPase activity was not seen in Sa FtsZΔC6.
source: However, this effect was not seen in Sa FtsZΔC6, suggesting that the last six C-terminal residues of Sa FtsZ is likely where the interaction with Sa GpsB occurs.
evidence: This is stated with reference to GTPase assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Addition of the Sa FtsZ octapeptide (383–390) to 15N-labeled Sa GpsB N-terminal domain results in a significant chemical shift perturbation to a small number of dispersed signals in the 1H-15N HSQC spectrum.
source: Addition of the octapeptide to 15N-labeled N-terminal domain results in a significant chemical shift perturbation to a small number of dispersed signals in the 1H-15N HSQC spectrum, suggesting that the interaction is highly localized and occurs through the coiled-coil region without disturbing the conformational heterogeneity of the dimer.
evidence: This is stated with reference to NMR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The interaction of Sa FtsZ peptide with Sa GpsB is highly localized and occurs through the coiled-coil region without disturbing the conformational heterogeneity of the dimer.
source: Addition of the octapeptide to 15N-labeled N-terminal domain results in a significant chemical shift perturbation to a small number of dispersed signals in the 1H-15N HSQC spectrum, suggesting that the interaction is highly localized and occurs through the coiled-coil region without disturbing the conformational heterogeneity of the dimer.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from NMR data.

claim: Only one of the Asn/Gln pairs of signals in the 1H-15N HSQC is shifted upon addition of the FtsZ peptide, while all other sidechain signals lie far from the binding site.
source: Indeed, only one of the Asn/Gln pairs of signals in the 1H-15N HSQC is shifted upon addition of the peptide, while in agreement with our model all other sidechain signals lie far from the binding site (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B), suggesting that Sa GpsB recognizes partner proteins in a conserved manner.
evidence: This is stated with reference to NMR data and structural model.

claim: Sa GpsB recognizes partner proteins in a conserved manner.
source: Indeed, only one of the Asn/Gln pairs of signals in the 1H-15N HSQC is shifted upon addition of the peptide, while in agreement with our model all other sidechain signals lie far from the binding site (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B), suggesting that Sa GpsB recognizes partner proteins in a conserved manner.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from NMR data and comparison with known structures.

claim: The cytoplasmic N-terminal mini-domains of PBP1, PBP2, PBP2a, and PBP3 have no affinity for Sa GpsB.
source: Although PBP1, PBP2, PBP2a, and PBP3 all have a cytoplasmic N-terminal 'mini-domain', none bear a GpsB recognition motif (Figure 4A). Using SPR, we confirmed their cytoplasmic mini-domains have no affinity for Sa GpsB, which is in agreement with the findings from previous bacterial two-hybrid assays (Steele et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with reference to SPR data shown in Figure 4A and citation to previous study.

claim: PBP4 has a short, cytosolic C-terminal mini-domain with the sequence of N-R-L-F-R-K-R-K, satisfying the consensus GpsB-binding motif (S/T/N)-R-X-X-R-(R/K).
source: Remarkably, PBP4, the only class C PBP encoded in the S. aureus genome, which purportedly functions as both a carboxypeptidase and transpeptidase PBP (Maya-Martinez et al., 2018), has a short, cytosolic C-terminal mini-domain with the sequence of N-R-L-F-R-K-R-K, satisfying the consensus GpsB-binding motif (S/T/N)-R-X-X-R-(R/K) found in S. aureus FtsZ and in orthologous PBPs found to bind to GpsB.
evidence: This is stated as a discovery from sequence analysis.

claim: The Sa PBP4 C-terminal octapeptide binds to Sa GpsB with a KD of 48.61±1.86 µM.
source: Next, using SPR, we demonstrate this Sa PBP4 C-terminal octapeptide binds to Sa GpsB with a KD of 48.61±1.86 µM (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated with reference to SPR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A potential interaction between Sa PBP4 and Sa GpsB was previously noted in a bacterial two-hybrid study.
source: Supporting this finding is a potential interaction between Sa PBP4 and Sa GpsB previously noted in a bacterial two-hybrid study (Kent, 2024).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Each GpsB dimer coordinates two others in a head-to-head arrangement in the crystal packing.
source: A key factor preventing the formation of this complex were the tight interactions forming at the crystal packing interface. By extending the asymmetric unit, we found each GpsB dimer coordinates two others in a head-to-head arrangement (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated with reference to crystal packing analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The head-to-head interaction involves the insertion of Arg and Lys residues from the membrane-binding loop into the PBP-binding site from the adjacent GpsB protomer, mimicking the binding mode observed between PBP mini-domains and GpsB in orthologous structures.
source: This involves the insertion of Arg and Lys residues from the membrane-binding loop into the PBP-binding site from the adjacent GpsB protomer, mimicking the binding mode observed between PBP mini-domains and GpsB in orthologous structures, such as Bs PBP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D; Cleverley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with reference to crystal packing analysis and citation to previous structure.

claim: The R24A mutation successfully disrupted the occluded crystal packing interface and allowed determination of a 2.40 Å resolution structure of Sa PBP4 peptide bound to Sa GpsB.
source: To do so, we generated an R24A mutant because of its central role in the head-to-head interaction and its distance from the PBP-binding groove. This point mutation successfully disrupted the occluded crystal packing interface and allowed us to determine a 2.40 Å resolution structure of Sa PBP4 peptide bound to Sa GpsB (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated with reference to crystallographic data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Arg425 and Arg428 of PBP4 are key components of the Sa PBP4-Sa GpsB interaction, where they form multiple hydrogen bonds with the main chain amides of Sa GpsB Ile13, Tyr14, Lys16, and the sidechain hydroxyl of Tyr26.
source: This structure clearly shows that two of these residues, Arg425 and Arg428, are key components of the Sa PBP4-Sa GpsB interaction, where they form multiple hydrogen bonds with the main chain amides of Sa GpsB Ile13, Tyr14, Lys16, and the sidechain hydroxyl of Tyr26.
evidence: This is stated with reference to crystal structure shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Arg425 and Arg428 of PBP4 form two salt bridges with the carboxyl sidechain of Asp32 of GpsB.
source: Furthermore, Arg425 and Arg428 form two salt bridges with the carboxyl sidechain of Asp32.
evidence: This is stated with reference to crystal structure shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Sa GpsB Asp36 plays a major role in stabilizing the PBP4 α-helix by forming two hydrogen bonds with the backbone nitrogen of Arg425 and Leu426.
source: Additionally, Sa GpsB Asp36 appears to play a major role in stabilizing the PBP4 α-helix by forming two hydrogen bonds with the backbone nitrogen of Arg425 and Leu426, an arrangement that is only possible when these two residues are part of an α-helix.
evidence: This is stated with reference to crystal structure shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The complex of Sa PBP4/Sa GpsB is very similar to Bs PBP1/Bs GpsB and is distinguished by the interactions of two Arg residues with the backbone and acidic sidechains lining the PBP-binding groove.
source: Overall, the complex of Sa PBP4/Sa GpsB is very similar to Bs PBP1/Bs GpsB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D) and is distinguished by the interactions of two Arg residues with the backbone and acidic sidechains lining the PBP-binding groove.
evidence: This is stated with reference to structural comparison.

claim: An AlphaFold2-Multimer model with the last six residues of FtsZ (S-R-R-T-R-R) was obtained and the nature of interaction resembles the Sa GpsB complex structure with the PBP4 peptide.
source: We further used AlphaFold2-Multimer to study the interactions between Sa GpsB and FtsZ (Evans et al., 2021). Although attempts using full-length GpsB and/or long segments of the FtsZ C-terminal domain did not provide satisfying results, a model with the last six residues (S-R-R-T-R-R) was obtained and the nature of interaction resembles the Sa GpsB complex structure with the PBP4 peptide (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated with reference to AlphaFold2 model shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The affinity of Sa FtsZ and Sa PBP4 derived peptides for Sa GpsBΔMADFL was significantly reduced compared to Sa GpsBWTFL.
source: Due to the apparent importance of the three-residue insertion at the midpoint of Sa GpsB, we also tested the affinity of Sa FtsZ and Sa PBP4 derived peptides against Sa GpsBΔMADFL. Using SPR we found that the affinity was significantly reduced for Sa GpsBΔMADFL compared to Sa GpsBWTFL (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated with reference to SPR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dose-dependent saturation was very weak (KD>200 µM) for Sa PBP4 (423–431) and Sa FtsZ (379–390) binding to Sa GpsBΔMADFL.
source: Dose-dependent saturation was very weak (KD>200 µM) for Sa PBP4 (423–431) and Sa FtsZ (379–390), which verged on being undetectable.
evidence: This is stated with reference to SPR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Titration of 15N-labeled Sa GpsBΔMAD1-70 with the Sa FtsZ383-390 peptide does not result in chemical shift changes to the GpsBΔMAD 1H-15N HSQC, but only in broadening of a small number of signals.
source: Additionally, titration of 15N-labeled Sa GpsBΔMAD1-70 with the Sa FtsZ383-390 peptide does not result in chemical shift changes to the GpsBΔMAD 1H-15N HSQC, but only in broadening of a small number of signals, which is consistent with the higher KD measured by SPR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated with reference to NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The deletion of MAD/MNN may disrupt interactions with α-helix 1 (residues 10–16), which may subsequently alter the size or shape of the PBP-binding pocket, thus reducing the favorable interactions that promote binding.
source: While these mutants demonstrate better thermal stability (Figure 2A), it is possible their deletion may disrupt interactions with α-helix 1 (residues 10–16; Figure 1B), which may subsequently alter the size or shape of the PBP-binding pocket, thus reducing the favorable interactions that promote binding.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on structural and binding data.

claim: The function of the hinge region and the flexibility it imparts remains unclear.
source: The function of this hinge region and the flexibility it imparts remains unclear, but its deletion increases thermal stability (Figure 2A) and weakens affinity for Sa FtsZ and Sa PBP4 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated as an acknowledgment of uncertainty despite experimental observations.

claim: The deletion of the hinge region increases thermal stability of GpsB.
source: The function of this hinge region and the flexibility it imparts remains unclear, but its deletion increases thermal stability (Figure 2A) and weakens affinity for Sa FtsZ and Sa PBP4 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated with reference to CD data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The deletion of the hinge region weakens affinity for Sa FtsZ and Sa PBP4.
source: The function of this hinge region and the flexibility it imparts remains unclear, but its deletion increases thermal stability (Figure 2A) and weakens affinity for Sa FtsZ and Sa PBP4 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated with reference to SPR data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The hinge region mutants are less functional in S. aureus and localize to the division site in both S. aureus and B. subtilis.
source: In S. aureus, we show that the phenotypes of ΔMAD (but not ΔMNN) mimic those of Sa GpsB (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C). Regardless, both ΔMAD and ΔMNN mutants localize to the division site in both S. aureus and B. subtilis suggesting they retain some level of affinity for their usual interaction partners.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of experimental observations.

claim: The hinge region in Sa GpsB may permit the protomers with different conformations within the complex to function independently from each other to allow for the fine-tuning of function and/or protein interactions.
source: Taken together, we believe that the hinge region in Sa GpsB may permit the protomers with different conformations within the complex to function independently from each other to allow for the fine-tuning of function and/or protein interactions.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of experimental data.

claim: The GpsB recognition motif on the C-termini of Sa FtsZ and Sa PBP4 involves the insertion of several Arg residues into the binding groove formed at the coiled-coil interface near the membrane-binding loop.
source: Next, we identified a GpsB recognition motif on the C-termini of both Sa FtsZ and Sa PBP4, leading to biophysical, biochemical, and structural experiments providing evidence of a direct interaction between these proteins and the N-terminal domain of Sa GpsB (Figure 3). This recognition motif, which is also present, but in the N-termini of Lm PBPA1, Sp PBP2a, and Bs PBP1, involves the insertion of several Arg residues into the binding groove formed at the coiled-coil interface near the membrane-binding loop (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Cleverley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with reference to structural data and citation.

claim: The repeated (S/T/N)-R-X-X-R-(R/K) GpsB recognition motif on the C-terminus of Sa FtsZ is unique to Staphylococci FtsZ and is absent/less conserved in other Firmicutes.
source: Our group previously found that Sa GpsB interacts with Sa FtsZ to regulate its polymerization characteristics, but the repeated (S/T/N)-R-X-X-R-(R/K) GpsB recognition motif on its C-terminus was not recognized until the work on such motifs in PBPs published by Cleverley et al., 2019. This motif is unique to Staphylococci FtsZ and is absent/less conserved in other Firmicutes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated with reference to sequence alignment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: It is unclear why the GpsB recognition motif is repeated on Sa FtsZ, since there is only enough area in the PBP-binding groove to accommodate a helix of eight to nine residues.
source: It is unclear why the GpsB recognition motif is repeated, since there is only enough area in the PBP-binding groove to accommodate a helix of eight to nine residues.
evidence: This is stated as an acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: It is possible that Sa FtsZ binds two Sa GpsB dimers simultaneously, given the putative arrangement of GpsB as trimer of dimers.
source: It is possible that Sa FtsZ binds two Sa GpsB dimers simultaneously, given the putative arrangement of GpsB as trimer of dimers (Cleverley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as speculation with a citation.

claim: The first GpsB recognition site on FtsZ may be occluded by the binding of other FtsZ interaction partners that are known to bind FtsZ through the C-term such as FtsA, EzrA, and SepF.
source: Alternatively, the first site may be occluded by the binding of other FtsZ interaction partners that are known to bind FtsZ through the C-term such as FtsA, EzrA, and SepF (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as speculation with a citation.

claim: The discovery of PBP4 binding to GpsB is notable because it was previously thought that only the N-terminal 'mini-domain' of transpeptidase PBPs (class A, class B) could bind to GpsB.
source: This discovery is notable because it was previously thought that only the N-terminal 'mini-domain' of transpeptidase PBPs (class A, class B) could bind to GpsB.
